verses.text: After five days, the high priest, Ananias, came down with certain elders and an orator, one Tertullus. They informed the governor against Paul.
When he was called, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying, “Seeing that by you we enjoy much peace, and that prosperity is coming to this nation by your foresight,
we accept it in all ways and in all places, most excellent Felix, with all thankfulness.
But, that I don’t delay you, I entreat you to bear with us and hear a few words.
For we have found this man to be a plague, an instigator of insurrections among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.
He even tried to profane the temple, and we arrested him.
None
By examining him yourself you may ascertain all these things of which we accuse him.”
The Jews also joined in the attack, affirming that these things were so.
When the governor had beckoned to him to speak, Paul answered, “Because I know that you have been a judge of this nation for many years, I cheerfully make my defense,
seeing that you can recognize that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship at Jerusalem.
In the temple they didn’t find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the synagogues, or in the city.
Nor can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me.
But this I confess to you, that after the Way, which they call a sect, so I serve the God of our fathers, believing all things which are according to the law, and which are written in the prophets;
having hope toward God, which these also themselves look for, that there will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust.
Herein I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men.
Now after some years, I came to bring gifts for the needy to my nation, and offerings;
amid which certain Jews from Asia found me purified in the temple, not with a mob, nor with turmoil.
They ought to have been here before you, and to make accusation, if they had anything against me.
Or else let these men themselves say what injustice they found in me when I stood before the council,
unless it is for this one thing that I cried standing among them, ‘Concerning the resurrection of the dead I am being judged before you today!’”
But Felix, having more exact knowledge concerning the Way, deferred them, saying, “When Lysias, the commanding officer, comes down, I will decide your case.”
He ordered the centurion that Paul should be kept in custody, and should have some privileges, and not to forbid any of his friends to serve him or to visit him.
But after some days, Felix came with Drusilla, his wife, who was a Jewess, and sent for Paul, and heard him concerning the faith in Christ Jesus.
As he reasoned about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix was terrified, and answered, “Go your way for this time, and when it is convenient for me, I will summon you.”
Meanwhile, he also hoped that money would be given to him by Paul, that he might release him. Therefore also he sent for him more often, and talked with him.
But when two years were fulfilled, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus, and desiring to gain favor with the Jews, Felix left Paul in bonds.

footnotes.content: Five days—a deliberate delay before the high priest brings formal charges. How patient Christ's enemies often are, arranging their accusations with care. Paul waits in custody, but Jesus is already preparing what His servant will say.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tertullus opens with flattery—'much peace,' 'prosperity,' 'foresight.' This is the orator's trade: honey before the blow. It reminds us that smooth words and worldly compliments are often the wrapper around an accusation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tertullus heaps gratitude on Felix as if the governor were nearly divine. The flesh loves to butter its judges before presenting the case. Yet no amount of courtly praise changes what truth is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The orator begs indulgence—'that I don't delay you'—then launches into his attack anyway. How often does malice wear the mask of brevity? We excuse a lie if it comes wrapped in apologies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'A plague,' 'instigator of insurrections,' 'ringleader of the Nazarenes.' Notice how accusers string together half-truths: yes, Paul disturbs the old order, but not through sedition—through the gospel. The charge is crafted to reach Felix's ear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They accuse Paul of trying to profane the temple. This cuts close to home—the temple is Jerusalem's heart. Yet Jesus Himself was accused of desecrating it, and His disciples will learn that the true temple is His body.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This verse contains no text in the record—a gap where words once may have stood. Sometimes the history itself shows us incompleteness, gaps where truth has been obscured or lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tertullus closes his accusation with an invitation: let Felix examine Paul himself. It sounds fair, but it masks the trap—the charge has already been planted, and examination often confirms what we've been told to believe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Jewish elders 'affirmed that these things were so.' Voices multiply around a lie, and soon it sounds like truth. This is the way of the world—a mob can convince us of almost anything if it speaks loudly enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul rises to answer, addressing Felix with respect: 'I know you have been a judge for many years.' He makes his defense 'cheerfully'—what courage it takes to speak truth with joy when enemies surround you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Not more than twelve days since I went up to worship.' Paul anchors his defense in a simple fact: twelve days from arrest to trial. In Jerusalem's narrow time frame, his accusers cannot hide their haste.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul says they found him neither disputing nor stirring up crowds in temple, synagogue, or city. He appeals to their own observation—truth asks only to be seen, not manufactured.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The simple truth: 'Nor can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me.' How strong is an innocent conscience before a judge. Paul stands in his own light, and no shadow falls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul confesses what he will NOT deny—he serves God according to the Way, believing all things in the law and prophets. He turns his accusation into testimony: yes, I follow Jesus, and I do so in the fullest obedience to Scripture.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul speaks of hope in resurrection, 'both of the just and unjust.' This is the hope that changes everything—not escape from death, but transformation through it. Felix hears it and begins to feel its power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'A conscience void of offense toward God and men'—Paul's defense rests on a clean heart. He has tried always to live at peace with both. This is what innocence looks like when it speaks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After many years, Paul came to bring gifts for the needy to his own nation. He speaks of generosity, of caring for his people—the works of a gentle heart, not a seditious one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul was found 'purified in the temple, not with a mob, nor with turmoil'—a detailed anchor. He was performing a ritual act of devotion, quietly, without crowd or chaos. This is the scene his accusers cannot honestly deny.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul points out the obvious: the accusers from Asia should be here if they had a case. They are absent—and their absence speaks louder than any words they've sent through Tertullus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul invites the council to speak of any injustice they found in him—a challenge that hangs in the air. Truth fears no question; lies hide behind silence and absence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The one thing Paul will not retract: 'Concerning the resurrection of the dead I am being judged before you today!' He stands on this confession—the heart of the gospel, the hope of all believers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Felix defers judgment, saying he will wait for Lysias. He 'had more exact knowledge concerning the Way'—perhaps he'd already heard its story. Delay can be a mercy when a judge's heart is not yet ready to decide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul is ordered kept in custody but with 'some privileges'—his friends may visit and serve him. Even in chains, he is not forgotten. The gospel travels through the bonds of friendship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Felix brings Drusilla, his Jewish wife, to hear Paul speak 'concerning the faith in Christ Jesus.' He chooses to listen, with his wife beside him. It is a strange moment—the accused becomes the teacher, the chains fade before the Word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul reasons about righteousness, self-control, and judgment to come—and Felix is terrified. The conscience knows when it has heard truth. Yet he dismisses Paul with 'when it is convenient,' and that moment never comes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Felix hoped Paul would bribe him for release. How revealing—the judge who heard the gospel's challenge turns it into a business transaction. He calls for Paul often, but always for the wrong reason.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two years pass. Felix yields to the next governor, leaving Paul in bonds—unjustly held to curry favor with the Jews. Looking back from a longer road, we see how often the innocent suffer when the powerful trade justice for convenience, yet how Christ's kingdom outlasts every empire that thought itself secure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
